extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, restorers, and designers of Gothic/medieval-style buildings
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for the form, proportion, and fitting of buttresses, doors, and windows (apertures) in masonry buildings, with emphasis on Gothic practice and structural/aesthetic fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of buttress
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct kinds; one, a narrow vertical pier, acting principally by its weight, and crowned by a pinnacle; the other, commonly called a Flying buttress, a cross bar set from such a pier (when detached from the building) against the main wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which type is required by the structural action needed: dead-weight piers for vertical load, flying buttresses as props/shores for lateral thrusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flying buttress must faithfully and visibly perform its office
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of the form of the flying buttress depends on its faithfully and visibly performing this somewhat humble office; it is, therefore, in its purity, a mere sloping bar of stone, with an arch beneath it to carry its weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design flying buttresses as clear structural props (sloping stone bars with an arch beneath). Avoid decorative perforation/traceries that weaken or disguise the structural role; prefer lightness only where sufficient for security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornament that sacrifices security
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems as if some security were sacrificed to ornament...the early traceries have been replaced by base flamboyant ones, utterly weak and despicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce ornamental perforations or traceries into structural members when it compromises strength; prioritize structural integrity over decorative refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buttress form: sloping or stepped according to height
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the common buttress must be familiar...sloping if low, and thrown into successive steps if they are to be carried to any considerable height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple sloping buttresses for low applications and stepped profiles when height requires. Maintain dignity by ensuring the form serves essential structural service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply buttresses only when structurally necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: In most modern Gothic, the architects evidently consider buttresses as convenient breaks of blank surface...They are even thought ornamental when they can be of no possible use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using buttresses as mere decoration or surface-breaks. Do not confuse buttresses with shafts or apply diminutive buttress-masses for purely vertical support; employ them only where they perform real function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indolent or vain use of buttresses
rubrics_metrics.description: No treason to Gothic can be greater than the use of it in indolence or vanity, to enhance the intricacies of structure, or occupy the vacuities of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from adding buttresses to conceal poor design or to fill compositional 'vacancies'. Let form follow genuine structural need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three main considerations for apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Respecting [doors and windows] there are three main points to be considered: 1. The form of the aperture (outline, size, forms of its sides). 2. The filling of the aperture (valves and glass, and their holdings). 3. The protection of the aperture (canopies, porches, and balconies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat aperture design by addressing outline/proportion, how it will be filled/secured, and what protective appliances or external features are needed—each in turn and in relation to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doors in roofed buildings should have arched headings
rubrics_metrics.description: The best heading must be an arch, because the strongest, and that a square-headed door must be wrong, unless under Mont-Cenisian masonry; or unless the top of the door be the roof of the building, as in low cottages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For doors with significant wall weight above, use an arch heading for structural strength; square-headed doors acceptable only in special low-roof or particular masonry conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum door proportions and geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: The apertures shall be at least above a man's height, with perpendicular sides (for sloping sides are evidently unnecessary, and even inconvenient), and level threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide doors at least over human head-height, with vertical jambs and level sills to ensure convenient passage; avoid unnecessary sloping jambs unless function requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bevel (splay) jambs for frequent ingress/egress
rubrics_metrics.description: When entrance and egress are constant...these angles, which would be worn away by friction, should at once be bevelled off, or, as it is called, splayed, and the most contracted part of the aperture made as short as possible...the bevelling may be very slight on the inside, but should be large on the outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For doors with rapid or frequent traffic, chamfer external jambs significantly (slight inside) to ease circulation; bevel the door arch correspondingly to avoid awkward sharp junctions and to present a smoother approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust door size and number to crowd usage and procession
rubrics_metrics.description: If entrance is required for multitudes at the same time, the size of the aperture either must be increased, or other apertures must be introduced...often many doors are by far the best arrangement...sometimes the purposes of the building require the large single entrance (processions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between multiple smaller doors or fewer larger doors based on anticipated circulation, processionary needs, and aesthetic/structural harmony with the building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of a principal entrance proportioned to building
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the entrances be single, triple, or manifold, it is a constant law that one shall be principal, and all shall be of size in some degree proportioned to that of the building...the width being the only useful dimension in a door...it is well to increase the height also in some proportion to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always designate one principal doorway and size entrances in proportion to the building's scale—width primary, with height adjusted for expression and to reduce wall weight above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Door jamb thickness proportional to door magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the height and size of the building, and therefore to the size of its doors, will be the thickness of its walls...the splaying or chamfering of the jamb of the larger door will be deepened, and, if possible, made at a larger angle for the large door than for the small one; so that the large door will always be encompassed by a visible breadth of jamb proportioned to its own magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure larger doors have visibly broader jambs/splays to match scale; treat deep jambs as decorative opportunities consistent with structural necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window classes: outlook vs inlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Window apertures are mainly of two kinds; those for outlook, and those for inlet of light, many being for both purposes...the sill of the windows...should be horizontal, for the convenience of leaning on it, or standing on it if the window be to the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify windows by primary purpose (view vs light) and design sill height, approachability, and jamb shaping accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlook windows: bevel to increase range of sight
rubrics_metrics.description: If the aperture be inaccessible, or so small that the thickness of the wall cannot be entered, the wall is to be bevelled on the outside, so as to increase the range of sight as far as possible...the bevelling will, if possible, be in every direction...but essentially downwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For outlook windows, bevel external jambs downward (and outward) to widen the external field of view; maximize approachability where feasible (or provide oriels/bows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inlet windows: shape and beveling aimed at admitting and directing light
rubrics_metrics.description: These windows...have their purpose to throw [light] in streams on particular lines or spots...the bevelling in the inlet window is a means not only of admitting the light in greater quantity, but of directing it to the spot on which it is to fall...no natural light will strike on the inlet window from beneath...the sill is to be flat, if the window be on a level with the spot it is to light; and sloped downwards within, if above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inlet windows to admit and direct light: outside bevel upwards to catch steep rays, internal slope/downward sills if window is above the target spot; avoid designs that produce harmful reflected light from beneath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window form: accept many shapes but avoid structurally weak or visually indecisive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Windows may be of any shape...yet the elliptical oval is generally an unsatisfactory form...all elongated forms are still more objectionable placed horizontally, because this is the weakest position they can structurally have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms that harmonize structural strength and optical effect (circles, pointed ovals). Avoid elliptical or horizontally elongated forms when they compromise strength or appear indecisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of recess (bevel) confers nobility and domestic dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The depth of recess which I have observed to be essential to nobility of external effect has also a certain dignity of expression, as appearing to be intended rather to admit light to persons quietly occupied in their homes, than to stimulate or favor the curiosity of idleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide deep window recesses in thicker masonry to convey dignity and measured domestic character; they also improve light control and privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Door fillings: use horizontal lintel to enable rectangular valves
rubrics_metrics.description: The arch-shaped head of the valves not only requires considerable nicety in fitting to the arch, but adds largely to the weight of the door...It becomes, therefore, a matter of true necessity so to arrange the doorway as to admit of its being fitted with rectangular valves...There is, therefore, no reason why it [the arch] should not be barred across by a horizontal lintel, into which the valves may be fitted, and the triangular or semicircular arched space above the lintel may then be permanently closed...This is the form of all good doors, without exception, over the whole world and in all ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where practical, deploy a horizontal lintel under the arch so door leaves can be rectangular and lighter; fill the tympanum above as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window filling materials: stone traceries, not wood or iron
rubrics_metrics.description: When windows are large...the sheet of glass requires the support of bars of some kind, either of wood, metal, or stone...Wood is inapplicable on a large scale...Iron is, however, fit for window-bars, and there seems no constructive reason why we should not have iron traceries...but...The window-bars must, therefore, be of stone, and of stone only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stone tracery for window bars in significant masonry architecture for permanence and compatibility; avoid wood for large windows; be cautious about iron traceries as they may not count as proper architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracery subordination principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the shape of the window...there are to be central or main bars; second bars subordinated to them; third bars subordinated to the second, and so on to the number required. This is called the subordination of tracery...All tracery, therefore, which is not subordinated, is barbarous, in so far as this part of its structure is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a hierarchical framework of bars: main central members heavier, secondary and tertiary bars progressively lighter, producing visual and structural unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bars direction and proportion: vertical preferred, oblong glass areas stronger
rubrics_metrics.description: A given area of glass...is stronger in its resistance to violence when it is arranged in a long strip or band than in a square; and therefore glass is generally to be arranged...in oblong areas: and if the bars so dividing it be placed horizontally, they will have less power of supporting themselves...As far, therefore, as the form of the window permits, they are to be vertical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide glass into oblong vertical panes with vertical stone mullions for greater resistance and slenderness; use cross bars only as necessary for supporting tall uprights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce cross bars to steady tall vertical mullions (usually up to two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when so placed [vertical], they cannot be trusted to support themselves beyond a certain height, but will need cross bars to steady them...However high the window, it is almost impossible that it should require more than two cross bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add horizontal support bars at intervals to brace long vertical mullions; typically one or two cross bars suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple tall windows are adjacent, bond piers with thicker cross-bars
rubrics_metrics.description: When tall windows are placed very close to each other for the sake of more light, the masonry between them may stand in need...The cross bars of the windows may then be thickened, in order to bond the intermediate piers more strongly together, and if this thickness appear ungainly, it may be modified by decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thicken cross-bars to structurally tie intermediate piers where windows are closely spaced; disguise necessary massing with appropriate decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inset and frame window bars into their own arch system for mutual support
rubrics_metrics.description: If we merely let the ends of the bars into the voussoirs of its heading, the least settlement of the masonry would distort the arch...Evidently our object should be to connect the window bars among themselves, so framing them together that they may give the utmost possible degree of support to the whole window head...Capital them; throw small arches across between the smaller bars, large arches over them between the larger bars...and we have a complete system of mutual support, independent of the aperture head, and yet assisting to sustain it, if need be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an internal framework of capitals and inter-arches so tracery supports itself and helps sustain the arch-head; pierce spandrils with circles to let light through while keeping structural cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular (wheel) windows require radial (spoke) tracery
rubrics_metrics.description: A small circle...is put into the centre of the window, large enough to give footing to the necessary number of radiating bars; and the bars are arranged as spokes, being all of course properly capitaled and arch-headed. This is the best form of tracery for circular windows, naturally enough called wheel windows when so filled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For round windows, provide a central ring with radiating stone bars (spokes) capitaled and arch-headed to secure footing and proper distribution of stresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural forms are founded on laws of gravity and cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: They are forms having essentially nothing whatever to do either with Goths or Greeks. They are eternal forms, based on laws of gravity and cohesion; and no better, nor any others so good, will ever be invented, so long as the present laws of gravity and cohesion subsist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design decisions should be founded on enduring structural laws rather than on mere historical imitation; prioritize form following fundamental physical requirements.
